- *Selection of the repair set.* Only items where the correct option is uniquely longest and a safe edit exists are retained: 306 of 1,664 candidates, with datasets contributing 0 safe edits (AMBOSS, MMMU-HM, MedXpertQA-MM have zero; Table 11). The results therefore rest on JAMA, MedThinkVQA and NEJM. Spatial repairs come almost entirely from JAMA and MedXpertQA-MM (Table 12; 47 + 48 of 101). The generalization to "six datasets" claimed in the abstract is not supported.
- *The reported drops are modest.* Effects of 3.5-6.6 pp are small relative to the 62.6% to 29.7% gaps used to motivate the problem. For the absolute/conspicuous family (−3.50 pp), most per-model intervals cross zero (Table 21), and the aggregate CI is wide ([−5.18, −1.79]). The conclusion that these cues are "behaviorally consequential" is acceptable for length gaps but weaker for the others.
- *No active control for a generic "any edit" effect.* There is no condition with equal-size neutral edits to distractors (e.g., paraphrase that does not alter the cue) to show that accuracy changes are specific to the cue and not caused by any rewrite or distribution shift. This matters because accuracy drops for nearly every model, including the weakest ones.
- *Pooled statistics.* The "17-config mean" averages highly correlated configurations (thinking/non-thinking modes of the same model are treated as separate). The CIs therefore treat configurations as exchangeable replicates, but this is not an independent sample of models. The paired bootstrap resamples items, which is fine, but the headline is an equal-weight average over a heterogeneous panel and is not a claim about any specific model.

**W3. The image-side claims are weak.** This is the part most relevant to "visual reasoning", and it is the least supported.
- The paper itself says image-hint results are small and model-dependent (Table 27: Δ from −0.05 to −3.75 pp on 200 pairs, and CIs are not given in the main text). Table 28 shows the MedGemma family at +0.23 pp. Natural-cue neutralization yields near-zero family means (−0.02 to +0.26 pp, Table 30).
- Image-text leakage (65 high-risk cases out of 13,940 images, of which 14-15 are repairable) and device cues (9 confirmed) are described as "rare", and have no performance analysis. The title and abstract nevertheless present visual-route shortcuts as a core finding.
- The visual-side edits (inpainting via an image generation model, best-of-five judged by an LLM) have no held-out check for artifacts that models could exploit. Only 46 edits were expert-reviewed.
- The prevalence counts in Section 5 (e.g., 5,645 "text residuals", 4,970 manual markups, 2,642 context features, 955 device/material cues across 13,940 images) come from a GPT-5.4-mini high-recall screen. They are not validated, so they may mostly be false positives. The Table 26 funnel shows 2,605 broad candidates and 1,088 strict, and the paper reports no precision estimate.
- Notably, the paper never shows an experiment in which the image is swapped, blanked or shuffled within the Full-input condition. That is the natural test of whether visual evidence is used. Image+Options (43.84%) is below full input but well above options-only. Image+Options is also higher than Full input on MedQA-MM (28.47% vs 26.59%). This is a surprising result that undermines the interpretation of the modality lattice, and the explanation offered (stem interference in 32/300 errors) is thin and mostly speculative.

**W4. MedQA-MM is under-validated and its headline numbers are circular.**
- It is built by filtering and repairing with the same signals later used to evaluate it (text-only, options-only, and the guessers). Text-only accuracy falling to 5.21% and options-only to 12.33% is therefore close to guaranteed by construction. It is not evidence that the subset measures image-grounded reasoning. The construction ("difficulty and visual-dependence scoring", "shortcut filtering or repair", "image-availability checks") is described only briefly in the main text, and it is not clear which models define "difficulty". If hard items were selected against strong models, then low accuracy partly reflects adversarial filtering. The 1,000 items are retained from 4,432 candidates (22.6%), and the filter targets the evaluated panels.
- Accuracies of 5% text-only and 12% options-only are well below chance (about 20%). A below-chance result is a sign of adversarial selection, which can create its own artifacts. A new "anti-shortcut" artifact would show up as models doing worse than random without the image.
- Absolute performance is low (GPT-5.4 36.9%, MedGemma-27B 9.3%; Fig. 8). The paper does not show that the benchmark is more valid. It could simply be harder or noisier (item/data issues are the largest error category, 29/70 = 41.4%). A benchmark with many flawed items cannot be called a better measure of visual reasoning.
- It is not released, and the paper itself says redistribution rights are unresolved (AMBOSS, JAMA, NEJM are audit-only, and MedXpertQA-MM image rights remain "to be confirmed"). A benchmark contribution that cannot be released has limited value to the community, and reproducibility is limited.
- No human (clinician) performance, and no estimate of the proportion of MedQA-MM items that a clinician could answer with and without the image, is given.

**W5. Heavy reliance on LLM judges and weak human validation.**
- Nearly every pipeline stage (cue screening, adjudication, repair, image-edit judging, rationale-based cue use and "bad-use" labeling, stem-interference judging) uses GPT models (GPT-5.4 and GPT-5.6-Sol).
- Human validation is limited. 150 option-form repairs were reviewed: 94.7% valid with 5.3% having "minor concern", and 38% only "partially improved". The reviewed set has no non-repaired controls, and annotators saw items labeled as repaired, so they were not blind. No inter-annotator agreement is reported for the repair-validation review (only the LLM-judge agreement, 92% with κ=0.703, for the stem-interference screen on 100 cases).
- The bad-use / cue-use metric (Section 3.5, Tables 27-31) rests entirely on model-written rationales judged by GPT-5.4. Rationales are known to be unfaithful, so the metric cannot support claims about "harmful reliance". The paper does say rationale judgments describe observable outputs, but the bad/cue ratio is then used to separate "awareness from harmful reliance" (Fig. 6) and to draw model-specific conclusions, which is overreach.
- The error taxonomy uses only 70 cases for the "development" split, from three models, so the percentages (e.g., 51.4% "visual or reasoning/integration") are very noisy and not reported with intervals.

**W6. Clarity, organization and consistency.**
- The paper is extremely dense with counts. Different denominators are used (7,706 / 7,715 / 7,722; 13, 16, 17, 19 configurations; 20 vs 10 repeats), and many numbers differ between analyses (e.g., 60 vs 65 "high-risk" image-text cases; 1,290 no-shortcut + 48 + 9 = 1,347). Appendix Table 4 reconciles some but not all of this. Per-analysis panels of 16-17 configurations differ in composition, which makes the cross-analysis comparison hard.
- The "aha" metaphor and the "two-aha" framing (Fig. 1) are decorative, and add no technical content. The paper concedes it is "shorthand".
- Several accuracies use "parser-oracle conventions" in some columns and "symmetric fixed parsers" in others (Tables 19-22 captions), so the destination columns cannot be reconciled with the accuracy columns. Parse failures are counted incorrect in some summaries (2.06% residual failure rate, 8,267 failures in 400,712 rows) and "salvaged" in others. It is unclear how much of the reported deltas arises from parsing differences between original and edited items. Edited long options may increase parse failures.
- Table 23's open-model mean excludes GPT rows, and the "reported accuracy" column has different meaning for the guesser row. The total in the abstract (62.63%) comes from a panel containing MedGemma and Qwen only, so the stated headline is not "frontier model" performance. The most capable evaluated model, GPT-5.4, reaches 73.3% on the pooled set.
- Figure 3 right-hand panels plot "drop magnitudes" (sign flipped) while the text uses signed changes, which is confusing. Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 are hard to read.
- Evaluating GPT-5.4 as repairer and evaluated model, plus a model "GPT-5.6 Sol" and Qwen3.5/3.6, makes the models in the study hard to reproduce. Most cited sources are accessed web pages, and the model identifiers are only available through APIs that may change. The data-generation code and the repaired items are not released at review time.

**W7. Related work and novelty.** Prior work already shows text-only and language-prior solvability of medical VQA and of multimodal MCQ benchmarks (e.g., the cited MIRAGE and MMMU-Pro, as well as work on VQA language priors). Prior work on item-writing flaws in medical MCQs is also extensive. The novelty here is the combination into one framework and the matched-repair experiments. The paper should more clearly distinguish what is new from what is confirmed. It would also help to compare directly with existing mitigation approaches such as option shuffling, filtering by adversarial models (as in MMMU-Pro's text-only filtering or MedXpertQA's design), and distractor augmentation. The paper claims that "shortcut-mitigated" MedQA-MM is a contribution, but it does not compare to the simpler baseline of MedXpertQA-MM or MMMU-Pro (both already designed to reduce text-only solvability).

## 4. Questions for the Authors

1. What fraction of correct full-input answers are (a) also correct under options-only or text-only, and (b) change after repair? Can you provide a per-item route decomposition rather than average deltas?
2. Does the length-gap effect persist when the edit is generated by a different model, or by human authors, and when the edited option is lengthened by content-neutral rewording versus informative content? Is there a control in which non-cue distractors receive equally sized edits?
3. What are the per-dataset effects of the three repairs? The three families come from different, mostly non-overlapping datasets. Does the pooled result hold within JAMA alone, for example?
4. How was MedQA-MM's "difficulty" defined, and which models were used for filtering? What are the below-chance text-only (5.21%) and options-only (12.33%) accuracies telling us? Is the subset adversarially selected against the evaluated models, and what happens with held-out models?
5. Why does Image+Options (28.47%) exceed full input (26.59%) on MedQA-MM, and does this also occur on the pooled audit for any model (see Table 23)? What does this say about the interpretation of "full input" as the intended route?
6. Can the image-hint and natural-cue effects be reported with CIs in the main text? Given the near-zero averages, what does the paper conclude about these routes?
7. What is the precision of the GPT-5.4-mini screens that generate the prevalence counts of 5,645, 4,970, 2,642 and 955? Was any sample verified?
8. How do parse-failure rates differ between original and edited items, and do the headline deltas survive when failures are excluded or handled symmetrically?
9. How would a real image-ablation test (blank or mismatched image within the full-input prompt) change the conclusions?

## 5. Ratings (EMNLP-style)

- **Soundness: 3 / 5.** The option-form matched-repair evidence for length gaps is reasonably careful. The central "reasoning inflation" claim, the image-side claims and MedQA-MM validity are not adequately supported. There are LLM-judge circularity concerns, confounded edits and thin human validation.
- **Excitement / Significance: 3 / 5.** The question is important and the audit is useful as a checklist and a methodology. The empirical findings are largely confirmatory, and some are modest in size.
- **Novelty: 2.5 / 5.** The combination and the matched-repair design are new. The individual insights (option cues, language priors, no-image solvability) are well known.
- **Reproducibility: 2.5 / 5.** Prompts are provided, which is good. The benchmark and repaired data are not released and rely on closed APIs and unreleased model versions, and the licensing status is unresolved.
- **Overall recommendation: 3 / 5 (Borderline; leaning weak accept for Findings, weak reject for the main conference in current form).**

## 6. Suggestions for Improvement

- Define reasoning inflation operationally and report it as a number (a per-item route decomposition), with uncertainty.
- Add placebo edit controls, human-written or cross-model edits, and per-dataset breakdowns for the repair experiments.
- Include genuine image interventions in the full-input condition (blank, mismatched, shuffled images), and report them next to the text-only and options-only ablations.
- Validate the screening pipelines with a human-labeled sample (precision and recall) and report inter-annotator agreement with blind, non-repair-labeled controls.
- Evaluate MedQA-MM on held-out models not used in construction, report human or clinician baselines, and compare against existing hard or filtered medical VQA benchmarks.
- Streamline the paper. Move the secondary analyses (device, image-text, SDOH) into the appendix or cut them, and put the strongest results (Tables 18-19, Fig. 4) first. Reduce the numeric bookkeeping and keep one consistent denominator for the main claims.
- Tone down the abstract and title: the image-side and device/context findings are curation-risk observations, not demonstrated causes of inflated scores.

**Confidence: 4 / 5.** I read the whole paper, including the appendices. I did not verify the numbers independently.

# Review: "From Visual Cues to Spoken Narration: Rethinking Audio Description"

## Paper Summary

The paper argues that automatic audio description (AD) should predict both *what* to describe and *when* to speak it, over long untrimmed movie clips. Prior work usually assumes an oracle window and treats AD as clip captioning.

The contributions are:

1. **LongLSMDC.** A benchmark built from full-length LSMDC movies, cut into clips of up to 8 minutes (~6.5 min on average, ~40 ADs per clip). Each AD can have a *visual cue window* (when the event is on screen) and a *spoken narration window* (the dialogue gap where it is voiced). The spoken windows were obtained from the LSMDC authors.
2. **Cue2Narrate**, a two-stage pipeline:
   - *Stage 1* is an audio-visual dual-head localizer. It is ActionFormer-style, with VideoMAE and log-mel features fused by additive pyramid fusion. One head predicts visual windows and the other spoken windows.
   - *Stage 2* is a LoRA-tuned Qwen VLM. It generates a one-sentence AD from frames in the predicted visual window. It is trained with SFT plus a Description Ranking Loss (DRL) that ranks the GT AD above a long caption produced by a frozen VLM.
3. **Results.**
   - Localization: +3.6 average mAP over a dual-head ActionFormer, +5.0 over audio-only and +11.8 over video-only. There is also transfer to CMD-AD and MAD-Eval.
   - Generation: modest CIDEr gains from DRL over an SFT baseline, under both GT and predicted windows.
   - A small human preference study against Shot-by-Shot.

## Summary of Strengths

- **Good task framing.** Separating *what* (visual cue window) from *when* (spoken narration window), and noting that the two are routinely offset, matches how AD is produced. Most prior AD work ignores this.
- **Useful resource.** A multi-segment, long-form benchmark with both window types is a real gap. The paired-supervision idea, where each head is trained on its own target, is sensible.
- **Thorough localization evaluation.**
  - It includes unimodal and naive-fusion baselines, a Gemini 2.5 Pro baseline, fusion ablations, per-duration analysis and per-tIoU breakdowns.
  - It also covers zero-shot and fine-tuned transfer to two other benchmarks.
  - Three-seed variances are reported, and they are small.
- **Honest about evaluation.** The paper states that text metrics are computed only on matched pairs and that GT→S2 and S1→S2 numbers are not directly comparable. It reports coverage separately in Table 5 and includes a failure-mode analysis, which is more candid than most.
- **Reproducibility effort.** Prompts, the evaluation protocol and a release plan are given. The Action-Score preprocessing is released so that metric needs no proprietary model.

## Summary of Weaknesses

### 1. The end-to-end setting is weakly evaluated, and the headline S1→S2 numbers are hard to interpret

- Table 5 shows that at tIoU 0.3 only 27.5% of predictions match a GT spoken window, so about 72% of predicted ADs are unmatched. Roughly 3.4 predictions are produced per true slot. At tIoU 0.5, precision is 21.2% and recall 73%.
- Table 4's text metrics are computed only on matched pairs, so they say nothing about the ~70% of generated ADs that are unmatched.
- There is no metric that combines localization and generation. Examples would be a caption-quality-weighted F1, or CIDEr with unmatched predictions and misses counted as zero.
- Without one, the claim of a "first benchmark for multi-segment AD generation" is only half-supported. The pipeline's realistic output (~3× over-generation) is never judged as a whole. The matched subset is also likely easier than average, which inflates CIDEr.
- The paper explains that annotators do not mark every usable gap. That is exactly why precision against GT is a poor proxy, and it argues for a different evaluation design rather than leaving the issue to an operating-point note.
- The visual window drives generation, but only the *spoken* window is evaluated end-to-end. Visual-window quality is never linked to caption quality. A clear experiment is a controlled ablation on the same matched set with (GT visual, GT spoken), (pred visual, GT spoken) and (pred visual, pred spoken). The current comparison confounds localization error with changing the evaluation subset (Sec. 5.2 acknowledges this).

### 2. Several claims are contradicted or only weakly supported by the paper's own tables

- **Which modality dominates.** Sec. 4.2 and Sec. 5.1 state that "video dominates visual cue window localization." In Table 2, audio-only ActionFormer beats video-only ActionFormer on the *visual* head (35.2 vs 32.0), as well as on the spoken head (39.1 vs 28.5). The "each modality dominates its regime" narrative (Fig. 4a) is shown only for a duration split.
- **The visual and spoken heads may learn largely overlapping targets.**
  - Fig. 3a shows that cross-head evaluation drops mAP by only ~4–5 points (~42 to ~38 and ~37). Taken at face value, that means the two target sets mostly overlap at tIoU 0.2–0.6.
  - The paper never reports offset statistics beyond "88% exhibit an offset". Missing are the distribution of onset and offset differences, the pairwise tIoU between paired windows, and the proportion falling before, during or after the dialogue gap.
  - A trivial baseline that predicts the spoken window and applies a learned offset, or a single-head model with two regressors, is not compared.
- **The Gemini baseline is not an informative comparison.**
  - Prompted zero-shot timestamp prediction is compared with trained localizers.
  - The Spectrogram baseline (1.4 mAP) is never defined. It is unclear what it does, and it is oddly far below audio-only ActionFormer at 37.1.
- **The architectural contribution is a small increment.** The gain over the naive-fusion dual-head ActionFormer is +3.6 mAP. The fusion ablation shows add vs. concat/avg differing by 1.5–2 mAP. The learned temporal position prior for the spoken head is never ablated. The Soft-NMS contribution is not ablated either.
- **MAD-Eval transfer is close to trivial.**
  - MAD-Eval clips are ~5 s with a single GT window. The 90.0 F1 is obtained under a top-1 protocol, with P = R = F1 by construction.
  - The comparison with CA3D's reported 65.3 F1 depends on matching tIoU thresholds and test splits exactly, which the main text does not demonstrate.
  - Table 2's 70.0 vs 63.7 mAP on MAD-Eval is a much smaller margin than the F1 headline suggests.

### 3. The generation contribution (DRL) is small and under-analyzed

- **Gains are small and mixed on the second backbone.**
  - On Qwen3-VL, GT→S2 CIDEr improves 36.0→37.3, and the three-seed std is ≤0.3.
  - On Qwen2.5-VL, Table 3 shows CIDEr +2.4 but Action Score *decreasing* (41.7→40.9) and the third metric column also decreasing (43.8→43.3). In Table 4, CIDEr changes by +0.5 while the other two metrics decrease (38.8→38.3, 37.3→37.0).
  - On CMD-AD (Table 3), Qwen2.5 CIDEr improves but Action Score decreases (35.4→35.0).
  - The text ("consistently improve CIDEr", "gain holds for Action Score") overstates the picture. Multi-seed results are given only for Qwen3-VL.
- **No comparison with natural alternatives.** DRL's negatives are long, generic VLM captions, so the loss is largely a length and style discriminator. Missing comparisons include:
  - a prompt or constrained-decoding baseline for concise output (the few-shot prompt is already in Appendix D);
  - a length-normalized or length-penalized loss;
  - unlikelihood training, DPO or another preference objective with the same negatives;
  - negatives from a different source.
  - λ = 0.2 and τ = 0.5 are not ablated. Negatives come from Qwen3-VL even for the Qwen2.5 backbone.
- **Stronger baselines are missing.** The "+ Cue2Narrate" rows are compared to an SFT baseline built by the authors, which is reasonable. Training-free AutoAD-Zero and Shot-by-Shot, however, are far below any fine-tuned model on LongLSMDC (14–17 vs 30–37 CIDEr), and the UniAD adaptation is out-of-domain by the authors' admission (10.1 CIDEr, no fine-tuning). These comparisons show the benefit of in-domain fine-tuning and say little about the method. On CMD-AD zero-shot, Shot-by-Shot (26.3) is above Cue2Narrate (25.1) on CIDEr.
- **Metric mismatch.** Gemini 2.5 Pro scores highest on LLM-Eval (2.80 vs 2.68 / 2.43) and much lower on CIDEr. The authors attribute this to AD "register", but this is presented as an explanation rather than tested. The LLM judge is LLaMA-3-8B, which is weak and unvalidated against human judgment on AD. CIDEr rewards n-gram overlap with a particular annotation style, which DRL is explicitly designed to push toward.
- **CMD-AD predicted windows.** The drop from 25.1 (GT) to 11.5 (predicted) CIDEr is large and is explained away as a distribution mismatch. Stage 2 is claimed to transfer, but predicted-window transfer is the practically relevant case.

### 4. Task and method concerns

- **Pairing of the two heads.** The heads predict independently, and each has its own Soft-NMS. The paper never explains how the i-th visual prediction is associated with the i-th spoken prediction at test time (Fig. 2 uses an "idx" notation). Pairing is central to the "paired window" claim.
- **No fit constraint.** The generated sentence is never checked for fit with the predicted spoken window or gap. Real AD must fit the gap (the speech-rate and length constraint). Stage 2 sees no gap duration, dialogue content or prior ADs (k = 0), and Stage 1 is not evaluated for overlap with actual speech. Overlap with dialogue is the stated constraint in the Introduction.
- **Stage 2 is purely visual.** It uses visual frames and a prompt, with no audio or dialogue. Calling the whole pipeline "audio-visual" overstates it. Frame sampling differs between training (F = 32) and inference (F = 64) with no justification. The paper acknowledges the limitations of independent generation and two-stage training.
- **Dataset construction.**
  - Only 37K of the 79K training annotations are paired. The paired set is also the only supervision preventing head collapse, and this is explained only in a footnote ("post-processing steps").
  - The unpaired subsets have different noise characteristics, and the spoken windows come from an unspecified alignment procedure and were obtained privately.
  - Clip boundaries are random (uniform 300–480 s), and an annotation is assigned by its midpoint, which can cut events at boundaries.
  - The validation set is only 170 clips (~8 movies?). The paper says "validation" but Fig. 9 says "Test". It is unclear whether there is a held-out test set, whether splits are by movie, and whether hyperparameters were tuned on the evaluation set.
  - Movie data from LSMDC is likely in the pretraining data of Qwen and Gemini, and contamination is not discussed.

### 5. Human evaluation and character bank

- The user study uses 100 clips with 20 sighted evaluators against a single training-free baseline (Shot-by-Shot), not against the SFT baseline or an ablation without DRL. The paper gives no inter-annotator agreement or significance test, and does not say how windows were supplied to the baseline. Preference margins are modest (e.g., 57/43 on coverage). The claim that this evaluates timing is not backed by the stimulus, since evaluators watch the video with the ADs rather than listening to AD mixed into the soundtrack.
- The character bank identifies the named character in only 70.4% of cases where a portrait exists, and no portrait exists for 16.6% of mentions. The +3.0 CIDEr gain from CharBank on Qwen3-VL (34.3→37.3) is larger than the DRL gain, but CharBank is an auxiliary component and its role in the headline numbers is unclear. Table 3's Cue2Narrate row includes CharBank while some baselines do not, and the text notes this only in passing.

### 6. Presentation

- Several table headers and captions are garbled or truncated. The third column in Tables 3 and 4 is unlabeled. Table 4's caption says "using [blank] 3 matching". Table 3's caption has "= Re-" followed by a blank. The Fig. 4a y-axis and caption are missing the metric name. Lines like "gain ... exceeds the seed-level std. by ∼4×" refer to unlabeled quantities. These make the generation section hard to verify.
- The Fig. 2 caption says "frozen LLM with LoRA-adapted projection", while the text says LoRA on the language model plus a trainable projection. "LLM" and "VLM" are used interchangeably for the negative-caption generator.
- Mean AP is defined as "per video, then averaged". This should be justified against the standard class-wise TAL protocol.
- The related work is missing Movie101/Movie101v2 (Yue et al.). It has a movie-narration task with temporal narration grounding, and it is directly relevant to the claim that "when" has not been addressed.
- The paper says 83.8K annotations include validation, but Table 1 lists LSMDC as 108.5K. The mean ADs per clip is given as ~40 in Table 1 and 29–40 in the appendix.

## Comments, Suggestions and Questions for the Authors

1. How are visual and spoken predictions paired at test time? Do the two heads share anchors, or is matching done post-hoc?
2. Please report offset statistics between paired windows (distribution of start and end differences, pairwise tIoU, fraction before, during and after the gap).
3. Add a single-head baseline (e.g., predict the spoken window plus an offset or a second regression branch) to show that two heads are needed.
4. Please add an end-to-end metric that penalizes unmatched predictions and missed slots, and a controlled GT / predicted-window ablation on the matched subset (see Weakness 1).
5. Show DRL against simple alternatives (prompt-only, length penalty, DPO or unlikelihood) and ablate λ, τ and the source of negatives. Give seeds for Qwen2.5-VL.
6. Why does audio-only ActionFormer beat video-only on the visual head? This conflicts with the stated modality roles.
7. Clarify train, validation and test splits (movie-level?), and whether hyperparameters were selected on the evaluation clips. Please discuss pretraining contamination.
8. A listening-based user study with blind and low-vision users is left out, which is understandable. A timing-aware evaluation that mixes the AD into the audio would still be valuable.
9. Please fix the garbled tables, figure labels and captions noted above.

## Ethics and Reproducibility Notes

- **Face recognition.** The character bank is built by running face recognition against IMDb actor portraits. Even if the released bank contains only character names, the pipeline performs biometric identification of real actors, and the portraits and derived features come from third-party sources. The Ethical Considerations statement ("no personal data about real individuals") is too brief. Consider discussing licensing of portraits, how the bank is released, and misuse potential.
- **Data access.** The data depends on restricted-access LSMDC material and spoken-window annotations obtained privately from the original authors, derived from copyrighted AD tracks. The release plan promises these under the original terms, but this cannot be verified at review time.
- The ethics section mentions demographic bias in VLM-generated descriptions but does not test for it.

## Scores

- **Soundness:** 3 (Acceptable). The core localization results look solid. Claims about modality roles, DRL and end-to-end quality exceed the evidence.
- **Excitement / Overall assessment:** 3 (Borderline; leaning toward acceptance as a resource and task-framing paper, but only after fixes). The reframing and benchmark are valuable. The method contributions are incremental, and the generation evaluation is partial.
- **Reproducibility:** 3. Details are given, but data access is restricted and some quantities are missing.
- **Ethical concerns:** Minor (face recognition and data licensing).
- **Confidence:** 4 (confident, but I did not check every figure value or verify cited numbers).

**EMNLP Review: "Structural Uncertainty from Self-Preference in Black-Box Language Models"**

---

**Paper Summary**

The paper proposes "structural uncertainty," a black-box uncertainty signal built from an LLM's preferences over its own sampled answers. For each question the method does the following:
- It samples N=5 responses, each from a different prompt template.
- For each of M=5 trials, it draws a random spanning tree over the responses and asks the same model for pairwise preference judgments along the N−1 edges.
- It fits a Bradley–Terry model (with L2 regularization) or TrueSkill to the sparse comparisons, and runs PageRank on the resulting dense win-probability matrix to get a ranking distribution π^(m).
- It computes the entropy of the mean ranking, H[π̄], as total structural uncertainty. It splits this into a "within-trial" term (the mean entropy of the per-trial rankings) and an "across-trial" term (the Jensen gap).
- It combines each component with answer-entropy self-consistency using fixed signs.

Experiments cover five LLMs and eight benchmarks. The authors report that the combined score gives the best or second-best selective-prediction AUC on several reasoning and knowledge tasks. They also report that the signal collapses to near-uniform on HotpotQA, and that within-trial and across-trial components correlate with accuracy in opposite directions on math.

---

**Strengths**

1. The idea of using the stability of self-preference rankings as an uncertainty signal is interesting. Sparse spanning-tree comparisons are a reasonable way to limit cost, and the entropy decomposition is clean.
2. The paper is candid about a failure regime. HotpotQA is reported as a negative result, and the randomization ablation includes a negative control (Table 3, bottom).
3. The analysis goes beyond headline numbers. It includes a length-bias study, an orthogonality analysis against SemanticU and Self-ConsU, a TrueSkill backend check, and a budget-matched comparison.
4. The limitations section is honest. It says the decomposition is empirical rather than causal and that the judge is the same model as the generator.

---

**Weaknesses**

**1. The decomposition's interpretation is not justified, and the paper's own evidence undercuts it.**
- StructU_within is the mean entropy of the per-trial PageRank distributions. That entropy is high whenever the BT fit on a tree yields small utility differences. On a tree, which fits perfectly, this is mostly determined by the judge's stated confidence (and by the L2 penalty with C=1), not by "candidate ambiguity."
- The paper itself notes that the judge's confidence is mostly ≤65 in uncertain cases. Within-trial entropy may therefore largely measure judge confidence calibration or verbosity, i.e. a verbalized-confidence signal in disguise. It is not clear that "ambiguity among plausible candidates" is what it captures.
- Because BT with only N−1 comparisons on a tree always fits a perfect ordering, the model-based "ranking distribution" depends heavily on the regularizer. The sensitivity analysis in Fig. 7 shows near-flat results for C≥1, but it covers only Math-Synth.
- A reader needs a direct comparison against much simpler baselines. Examples include mean judge confidence, the fraction of preference reversals across trials, and Kendall-τ variance across trials. Without these, the BT+PageRank machinery is not shown to be necessary.
- A related point is that the BT-fitted utility in Eq. (2) uses only comparisons where "winner direction" is known. The text says confidences are used "optionally." Appendix C states that confidences are used by TrueSkill "but not Bradley–Terry." This is inconsistent with the main text and unclear about what BT actually consumes. If BT ignores confidence, the within-trial entropy for BT comes from the L2 penalty and the tree topology alone.

**2. The "complementarity" and "orthogonality" claims are weakly supported.**
- The method is built from N=5 samples, each generated with a different prompt template. This diversity is itself a source of signal, and the baselines (Self-ConsU, SemanticU) are computed from the same five samples. The comparison is therefore not about preference structure versus dispersion in isolation.
- The hybrid adds a second source of information (M·(N−1)=20 additional LLM calls) to a baseline that has only the N=5 samples. The budget-matched comparison is only one configuration (DeepSeek R1, AIME-25), and the margin is small (0.728 vs 0.717). No variance or confidence interval is given, and the dataset has only 30 questions.
- A fair comparison would give the baselines the same compute budget on all benchmarks. Examples are Self-ConsU with N=25, a SemanticU or verbalized baseline with matched calls, and a pairwise-judge baseline that does not use the structural decomposition.
- Self-ConsU with N=5 has at most 6 distinct entropy values. On Math-Synth, MATH-500 and other tasks where answers agree, it is highly tied, so any continuous signal can gain from tie-breaking alone. This is a plausible alternative explanation for the "hybrid gains," and the paper does not rule it out. An ablation would be to add a random continuous perturbation or a simple confidence-based tie-breaker to Self-ConsU.
- Near-orthogonality with SemanticU (median |ρ| = 0.10) only shows the signals are different. It does not show they are useful. A signal uncorrelated with the baseline can be noise, and the randomization ablation only partly addresses this.

**3. The fusion rule is tuned post hoc using the test results.**
- Eqs. (7)–(8) use sign conventions chosen "globally" from the observed correlation with accuracy on the same evaluation data (SU_a is added, SU_w is subtracted). This is not a pre-specified method: the sign for SU_w is "positive on reasoning tasks," which was found empirically.
- On the knowledge and factual tasks the sign of the correlation is not stable (Fig. 5 shows mixed signs on HotpotQA and TruthfulQA and weak results on MMLU-Pro), so the fixed rule applied to those tasks is not principled.
- The fixed-sign fusion also makes the method hard to use in a new domain. A practitioner cannot know the sign without labeled data, which defeats the purpose of unsupervised uncertainty estimation. The 20-question pilot proposed for detecting collapse needs labels or at least a diagnostic, and the paper does not make clear what labeled data it assumes.
- The "pilot" detector claims ≥98% accuracy, but it appears to be evaluated on the same 8 benchmarks (collapse vs. not-collapse), with only one collapse benchmark (HotpotQA, and arguably TruthfulQA). This is effectively a one-vs-rest classification of datasets, with very few positive examples. The 98% figure is not meaningful as stated.
- There is no fusion with principled alternatives, such as logistic regression on both components trained with cross-validation, or a simple sum of ranks. These would show how much of the gain depends on the hand-picked signs.

**4. Statistical rigor and presentation of results.**
- Table 1 reports single-run numbers, with no confidence intervals or significance tests. Many of the differences that decide bold and underline marks are about 0.01–0.02. The datasets also vary widely in size (AIME-24/25 have 30 questions each; AMC-23 has 40). On these, Sel-AUC differences are well within noise.
- In several cells (for example the AIME-24/25 rows for Amazon Nova Premier and Qwen 3 32B), the dashes in parentheses show that AUROC is undefined because there are no positives or negatives. Sel-AUC there rests on very few correct answers.
- Table 5 shows very low accuracies for Nova Premier (14–16%) and Qwen on AIME (14.7–20.7%) as well as Math-Synth (29.0, 21.7). The largest reported gains ("Qwen on AIME-25: +12.0%, Nova on AMC-23: +13.4%") come exactly from these low-accuracy, tiny-sample regimes, where Sel-AUC is highly unstable and mostly reflects the accuracy base rate.
- The definition of the target is odd: "robust failure" is defined as p̂_corr < τ with τ=1.0. This labels any question with at least one wrong response out of five as a failure. This is a strong and unusual choice. It conflates "model is unreliable on this question" with "the question is wrong", and in the text it is unclear whether Sel-AUC is computed against the correctness of the final answer or of this stochastic label. Appendix D.4 gives τ=1.0, 0.8, 0.6, but the main evaluation never evaluates the standard setting (correctness of a single answer or majority-vote answer).
- The text says "Spearman correlation, AUROC, and Sel-AUC," but the main table gives only Sel-AUC and AUROC. The meaning of "Sel-AUC" (risk–coverage area, where lower is better) versus its use as "higher is better" in the table is confusing.
- Some claims in the text do not match the tables. For example, the text says the combined estimator is highest or second-highest on "MMLU-Pro, TruthfulQA," yet Table 1 shows Self-ConsU or other baselines winning or tying in many TruthfulQA cells because all signals are saturated (≈0.99). The claim "gains are consistent across reasoning and knowledge benchmarks" is overstated given Fig. 4, where several cells are near zero or negative.
- Standard UQ baselines are missing. These include semantic entropy with NLI clustering (Kuhn et al.; Farquhar et al.), P(True)-style or verbalized baselines in their standard form, and an LLM-as-judge confidence baseline. SemanticU as implemented (embedding distance with KaLM) is weak, and the paper itself says it is the weakest baseline. Recent comparison-based baselines (Shrivastava et al., 2025; Lyu et al., 2025) are cited but not compared against, even though they are the closest related work (pairwise self-preference to estimate confidence).
- The VerbalizedU baseline is a separate verifier call (a "verifier LLM V" outputs PASS/FAIL plus confidence), not the standard "ask the model for its confidence." This is a different method from the one cited (Tian et al.; Xiong et al.), and it is unclear whether V is the same model.

**5. The choice of benchmark and experimental design limits generality.**
- Math-Synth is the paper's own synthetic benchmark. It is generated by Claude 3.7 Sonnet, which is closely related to one of the evaluated models (Claude Sonnet 4.5). The questions are nested-negation arithmetic problems. The main qualitative analysis (Appendix E.3) relies on this dataset, and the failure modes there (miscounting negations) are quite narrow. The headline gains are strongest on it, which limits how much can be inferred.
- The "no collapse on reasoning, collapse on retrieval" story rests on a single factual-retrieval dataset (HotpotQA), with TruthfulQA behaving differently (saturated). The explanation offered, that retrieval prompts elicit "structurally homogeneous" reasoning chains, is not tested. An alternative is that answers on HotpotQA are short spans, so judging between them is near-ties. A direct test would measure the lexical or semantic diversity of the candidates, or the judge's confidence distribution, and check whether collapse correlates with them across datasets.
- N=5 prompts with distinct "reasoning strategy" templates mean candidate diversity is induced by the prompt, not by sampling. The paper says increasing N to 10 "degrades performance" and attributes this to "high-temperature noise." However, N=10 is shown only on AIME with 30 questions (Fig. 8), and the claim is not supported with a controlled analysis. This is surprising for an ensemble-style method, and it likely signals an instability in the metric.
- There is no analysis of how the prompt templates themselves affect the results. Since uncertainty is entropy over rankings, it may be driven by which template is stronger. If templates have systematically different quality (for instance, R4 "no verification"), the judge's consistent preference for R1 over R4 is a template effect and not a question-level uncertainty signal. The appendix examples show exactly this ("explicit self-verification valued over conciseness"), which suggests that the preference is largely stylistic, in conflict with the claim that "structurally diverse solution paths enable meaningful discrimination."

**6. Theory and framing are overstated.**
- The "Jensen gap" decomposition H[π̄] = E[H[π^(m)]] + I is the standard mutual-information decomposition of epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty, as in Kendall & Gal and Abbasi Yadkori et al. Applying it to ranking distributions is a fairly direct reuse, not a new decomposition. The paper should be clearer about this.
- Calling the two terms "ranking instability" and "candidate ambiguity" is an interpretation. As noted above, there is little evidence for it beyond two illustrative figures (Fig. 3), which show hand-drawn scenarios and not measured data.
- PageRank over a BT win-probability matrix, with a damping factor of 0.85 and a uniform teleportation vector, adds a non-trivial smoothing toward uniform. Part of the "near-uniform collapse" on HotpotQA may be a mechanical result of this damping, and does not necessarily mean that "preferences are uninformative." The paper reports that PageRank adds only +0.015 Sel-AUC and does not report what happens with a simpler, more direct aggregate (for example, the BT softmax over θ, or the Borda count).
- The maximum possible entropy is log 5 ≈ 1.61. Figure 6b shows the HotpotQA within-trial entropy clustered at 1.60 for both correct and incorrect answers. That is consistent with the damping and L2 effects, which push the distribution toward uniform whenever judge confidences are near 50–60. This is a more mundane explanation than "the model is indifferent between all five responses."
- The paper claims the method "does not require model internals" and calls itself "orthogonal" to dispersion. However, the Related Work has no direct comparison with the closest black-box preference-based work (Shrivastava et al., 2025; Lyu et al., 2025; Zheng et al.-style LLM-as-judge confidence), so the positioning of novelty is incomplete.

**7. Reproducibility, anonymity, and presentation issues.**
- Key details are in the appendix, including the prompts and the judge's structured output. The main text should state clearly what the model sees when comparing (whether it sees the reasoning chains, only final answers, or both), since this determines whether the signal is about answers or style.
- Position bias in pairwise judging (order of the two responses) is not discussed. With N−1 comparisons per trial and random trees, order effects could produce the "instability" attributed to preference structure. Temperature 0 judging makes position bias deterministic per pair, but different trees with different pair orderings could still produce it. No randomization of presentation order is described.
- The text says Wilson's algorithm gives uniform spanning trees, but with N=5 there are only 5^3=125 labeled trees. With M=5 trials, the diversity of trees is small, and the same tree can occur twice in a question. This should be discussed. At temperature 0, repeating the same edge gives the same judgment, so across-trial variation can only arise from different edges (different pair contexts). The paper never shows that the judge's output varies for reasons other than the tree.
- The across-trial term is therefore partly a function of the number of distinct edges sampled. With 4 edges per tree out of 10 possible pairs and 5 trials, many pairs are queried more than once, and some never. The "instability" measures how the BT fit changes when different subsets of pairwise judgments are used. This is a measure of the intransitivity or inconsistency of the judge on a given question. If so, this should be stated and measured directly (for example, with a cycle count on the full tournament).
- The paper reports that the length-bias analysis was only on MATH-500. The reported control (partial correlation, "62% survives") is only linear.
- The claim "62% of the StructU–accuracy relationship survives" averages over very different values (19% to 90%). For DeepSeek R1 only 19% survives, and for GPT-OSS 64%. The headline "length explains almost none of the signal" is true only for Claude.
- Cost is a substantial limitation: 5 generations plus 20 judge calls per question, against 5 generations for the baselines. The latency argument (judgments are cheap) is not quantified in tokens or dollars, and the comparison in "Cost and Budget-Matched Comparison" is limited to one model and dataset.
- Several statements are repeated in different sections (collapse regime, the 98% detection), and Appendix D.1 and D.2 have the same title ("Full Results: TrueSkill + PageRank"). Table 22 and Fig. 10 are referenced but not included in the version I received (the PDF has 20 pages and the appendix is cut off at Appendix E.3.2). I could not verify the claims that rely on them, including the budget-matched comparison, the near-orthogonality analysis (E.8), the length analysis (E.9), and the bootstrap pilot (E.10).
- The paper uses non-public or very recent models (Claude Sonnet 4.5, Nova Premier), with a closed-source judge, so results may not be reproducible. Using a Claude 3.7 model to generate the benchmark is a further dependence. Anonymization appears fine.

---

**Questions for the Authors**

1. What is the exact input of the BT fit: binary winners only, or confidence-weighted? How different are the results if you replace the BT+PageRank pipeline with the mean judge confidence, or with the fraction of tree edges that flip direction across trials?
2. How are Self-ConsU ties handled when computing Sel-AUC? Does the hybrid gain persist when a simple continuous tie-breaker is added to Self-ConsU?
3. Why is the evaluation target p̂_corr < 1.0? What are the main results when the target is the correctness of the majority-vote answer or of a single answer?
4. Is the sign convention in Eqs. (7)–(8) chosen using the same data on which Table 1 is reported? What happens with a cross-validated learned combination?
5. Do you randomize the presentation order of the two responses in each pairwise judgment? If not, how much of the across-trial variation is due to position bias?
6. How many distinct spanning trees (and distinct edges) actually appear across the M=5 trials per question on average?
7. Can you provide confidence intervals (bootstrap over questions) for Table 1 and Fig. 4, especially for AIME and AMC?
8. Is the collapse on HotpotQA due to the judge being indifferent, or to short answers where preference is ill-defined? Does TruthfulQA, which is also factual, show the same behavior? (Table 1 suggests it does not.)
9. Why does performance degrade when N increases from 5 to 10? This seems at odds with the method being a good uncertainty signal.

---

**Overall Assessment**

*Soundness: 2.5/5.* The core idea is interesting and the analysis is more thorough than usual. The evidence for the central claims is not strong enough yet. The interpretation of the two components is not validated against simpler alternatives. The hybrid is tuned post hoc and compared against baselines with a lower budget and tie issues. The results come with no uncertainty estimates on small benchmarks. The evaluation target (τ=1.0) is non-standard.

*Excitement / Novelty: 3/5.* Using self-preference stability as a black-box signal is a fresh angle. The decomposition itself is a standard one. The empirical contribution would be stronger if the specific advantage over closely related comparison-based confidence methods were shown.

*Clarity: 3/5.* The paper is mostly readable and well illustrated. There are inconsistencies about whether BT uses confidence scores, repeated claims, and an abstract that overstates the "complementary" result relative to Table 1. The main text relies on appendix material that is truncated or missing from my copy.

*Reproducibility: 3/5.* Prompts, decoding settings and algorithms are described. Closed models, a self-generated benchmark and missing details about judge input and ordering limit reproduction.

**Recommendation: Borderline (leaning weak reject for the main track; would be a solid weak accept or Findings paper with the changes below).**

**Main changes that would raise my score:**
- Add the simple baselines (mean judge confidence, preference-flip rate, cycle or intransitivity counts, tie-broken Self-ConsU).
- Add compute-matched baselines on every benchmark.
- Report bootstrap confidence intervals, and use a standard correctness target.
- Replace the hand-set signs with a cross-validated combination.
- Control for position bias and template effects.
- Test the "structural homogeneity" explanation of HotpotQA directly.
- Add at least one more non-synthetic factual and one non-synthetic reasoning benchmark with larger test sets.

**Ethics / Limitations:** The limitations section is adequate, though it should also mention evaluation on small test sets and the dependence on a same-model judge. I have no ethical concerns.

# Review of "CATMark: A Context-Aware Thresholding Framework for Robust Cross-Task Watermarking in Large Language Models"

## Paper Summary

The paper proposes CATMark, a logit-bias (KGW-style) watermark with an adaptive entropy threshold for generation.

- **Generation:**
  - Each step's logit vector is compared by negative KL divergence to a set of online "prototype" logit vectors, which are updated by a running average.
  - The token is assigned to the best prototype if the similarity is at least α. Otherwise a new cluster is created.
  - Each cluster keeps a history of token entropies. The watermark threshold for that cluster is the q-quantile of this history, with q = f(mean entropy) = exp(−mean entropy).
  - Only tokens whose entropy exceeds the threshold receive the green-list bias δ.
- **Detection:**
  - Detection uses a single global threshold computed the same way over the whole sequence.
  - It applies an EWD-style entropy-weighted z-score over the tokens above that threshold.
- **Theory:**
  - Theorem 1 says that excluding low-spike-entropy tokens raises a lower bound on the z-score.
  - Theorem 2 is a DKW-based argument that the quantile threshold covers the "rejection region".
- **Experiments:**
  - Models are Qwen2.5-Coder-14B and Qwen2.5-14B, with Llama-3.1-8B in the appendix.
  - Datasets are HumanEval, MBPP, MATH-500 and StackEval, plus a small C4 check.
  - Baselines are KGW, SWEET (two fixed thresholds), AW, CSW and EWD.
  - The paper also reports ablations, back-translation and paraphrase attacks, and a runtime comparison.

## Strengths

1. The problem is well motivated. A single global entropy threshold is a real limitation when code, comments and prose are interleaved in one output, and mixed-modality outputs are an increasingly common use case.
2. Making the threshold data-driven, without a hand-calibrated per-task value, is a practical idea. The overhead is reported honestly: about 3% in generation time and about 20% in detection time.
3. The paper includes several useful analyses:
   - an ablation separating clustering from entropy-weighted detection (Appendix D);
   - a sensitivity analysis over (α, ρ);
   - a study of the choice of f (Appendix E);
   - a direct comparison of global versus cluster-based detection (Table 2). The authors admit the cluster detector is worse and use this to justify their design.
4. The limitations section is candid about redundancy-injection attacks and short sequences.

## Weaknesses

### 1. The theory does not support the claims

- **Comparing lower bounds is not comparing detection power.** The proof of Theorem 1 (Appendix G) compares a lower bound on the z-score of CATMark with a lower bound on the z-score of EWD.
  - A larger lower bound does not imply a larger actual z-score, or better TPR.
  - The bound itself rests on Kirchenbauer's Lemma, which lower-bounds the expected green probability. It is applied to the expected numerator only, and the variance is treated as fixed.
  - The "provably higher" wording in Section 3.3 and the abstract is therefore overstated.
- **The theory analyses a different quantity from the algorithm.** The theorems are stated in terms of spike entropy S and the boundary S* = γ + (1−γ)e^{−δ}. The algorithm thresholds on Shannon entropy H. No link between H-quantiles and the S* region is given.
- **Theorem 2's key condition is assumed, not shown.**
  - The condition f(μ_k) ≥ F_k(S*) + ε is not verified for f(x) = e^{−x}. F_k is unknown, so nothing guarantees it holds for any cluster.
  - DKW assumes i.i.d. samples. The entropy history is a non-stationary, autocorrelated sequence from a growing prototype, and the history is generated by the watermarked model itself.
  - The theorem is about per-cluster thresholds τ_k. The deployed detector does not use per-cluster thresholds (Section 3.2). Neither theorem describes the detector that is actually evaluated.
- **Generation and detection thresholds do not match.** Tokens are watermarked at generation when H_t exceeds a cluster-specific τ_k. At detection the set I uses a different global τ. Tokens that were watermarked but fall below the global τ are dropped. Tokens that were not watermarked but exceed it are counted. This dilutes the signal and breaks the clean hypothesis-testing story.
- **The null distribution is not justified.** Weights W_t = H_t are computed from the observed text, and the standard z-score assumes fixed weights. Entropy of each token depends on the preceding (possibly green-biased) context. The paper reports no empirical check of the false-positive rate at the chosen z-threshold. It reports only AUROC and TPR at a 5% FPR constraint, which are ranking metrics.

### 2. The method's design is heuristic and its central premise is not validated

- **The choice f(x) = e^{−x} is ad hoc.**
  - It depends on the units of entropy (nats versus bits) and on vocabulary size.
  - Appendix E shows that the reciprocal function gives 0% TPR and the sigmoid is intermediate, so performance is quite sensitive to a hand-picked function. This contradicts the "no tuning" claim.
  - α = −2 and ρ = 5 are also fixed by hand. The same values are reported for all tasks and models, but there is no evidence they transfer.
- **No evidence that clusters correspond to semantic or task states.**
  - Averaging raw logits into prototypes and comparing softmaxes by KL is a very coarse signal. Logits of a code token and a comment token at different positions need not be systematically separable.
  - The only evidence is Figure 4b (proportion of "pure" categories versus α) and an illustrative Figure 2. There is no purity or NMI analysis against ground-truth segment labels (code versus comment, formula versus narrative). There is no report of how many clusters are created (K) or how K grows with length.
  - The method may simply act as a per-sequence adaptive entropy cut-off, with the "semantic state" interpretation being unsupported.
- **The claim of "no pre-defined thresholds or task-specific tuning" conflicts with the algorithm.** Algorithm 1 lists the categories as "Globals … per task, initially empty". It is unclear whether prototypes persist across prompts and samples.
  - If they do, the output for one prompt depends on others in the batch or run, which hurts reproducibility and could leak across users.
  - If they do not, short outputs have little history. ρ = 5 means the first tokens of each cluster are watermarked unconditionally (τ = 0), which is exactly the failure case for code.
- **Cost scales poorly.** Each step computes KL against K full-vocabulary prototypes (|V| ≈ 150k for Qwen). K is unbounded. Runtime is reported only for HumanEval-length outputs (~550 tokens) on one GPU.

### 3. The empirical gains are small, inconsistently reported, and sometimes contradicted by the paper's own tables

- **No unwatermarked reference.** Table 1 has no non-watermarked row for Pass@1, METEOR, BERTScore or the StackEval scores. Without it, one cannot judge how much quality is lost, or whether "improves text quality" means "less degradation than KGW".
- **Pass@1 equals SWEET-1.2 on HumanEval, and gains elsewhere are tiny.**
  - HumanEval Pass@1 is 82.3 for both CATMark and SWEET-1.2. SWEET-1.2 is better on METEOR and BERTScore (25.5 and 88.2 versus 24.2 and 88.1). MBPP Pass@1 is 51.6 versus 51.5.
  - SWEET-1.2's weaker detection comes from a threshold chosen arbitrarily (0.6 and 1.2), not calibrated as SWEET prescribes. Detection gains over the strongest baselines are about 1 point of AUROC. For example, on HumanEval CATMark has 97.0 versus 96.4 for EWD, and on MBPP 93.4 versus 92.5.
  - CATMark's HumanEval/MBPP TPR is higher than most baselines, but on MBPP its AUROC and TPR are below SWEET-0.6 (91.7 AUROC, 65.8 TPR). Table 1 shows 67.2 TPR for CATMark.
- **Claims of "highest detection across all tasks" are not supported by the paper's own tables.**
  - In Table 6 (Llama), CATMark has lower TPR than EWD or SWEET-1.2 on HumanEval (90.2 versus 93.9 and 92.7) and lower AUROC than EWD on HumanEval and MBPP. Yet Appendix C says it achieves "optimal performance in both dimensions".
  - In the ablation (Table 7), on MBPP the QBT and QBT+EWD variants have higher AUROC (96.4 versus 93.4) and much higher TPR (85.0 and 85.4 versus 67.2) than full CATMark. This means the clustering component actively hurts detection on that dataset. The text only says clustering "preserves quality".
- **The ablation values are puzzling.** QBT alone gets 46.0 Pass@1 on MATH-500 and 48.7 on MBPP, which is far below KGW (68.6 and 50.5) and every other baseline. A quantile threshold that skips some tokens should be no worse than KGW, which watermarks all tokens. This suggests a bug or a poorly specified QBT variant. The whole quality story then rests on QBT being a weak straw man.
- **Inconsistent numbers across tables.**
  - Table 1 (MATH-500, no attack) has AUROC of 85.0 for KGW and 94.3 for SWEET-1.2. Table 4 ("before attack") has 90.7 and 96.4.
  - Table 2 "after attack" for the global detector is 93.5/77.3. Table 4 "after attack" for CATMark is 91.9/76.0, from a different attack. These may be different attacks, but nothing explains the other discrepancies.
  - Table 3 reports PPL "3.210" for two methods, apparently copy-pasted. Table 8 has an unlabeled extra column.
- **Statistics.** The "±" values are not defined (seeds? sampling runs? bootstrap?). Std values of 0.1 on 164 HumanEval problems and 0.0 on StackEval are implausibly small unless decoding is nearly deterministic. No significance tests are given, yet the abstract says "significantly improves". Decoding hyperparameters (temperature, top-p, number of samples for Pass@k) are not stated in the main text.
- **The LLM-judge evaluation is fragile.**
  - StackEval quality and code-comment consistency are scored by DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Differences are modest (for example 2.72 versus 2.29–2.55). The StackEval ablation shows QBT at 2.03 and QBT+CAC at 2.72, a very large swing that suggests judge noise or length effects.
  - No judge-validation, human check, or second judge is reported, and the judge sees watermarked outputs of different lengths.
  - Table 9 differences are 0.02–0.1 points, with SWEET-1.2 winning ACR on MBPP. The conclusion that watermarking causes no systematic loss is not statistically supported.
  - The StackEval PPL of 1.95 is identical for almost all methods, so it is uninformative.

### 4. The "cross-task" evaluation does not test what is claimed

- Each dataset is run separately. The paper does not build truly interleaved or switching prompts (for example code, then prose, then formulas, with multiple task switches inside one response), and it does not measure per-segment detectability or quality.
- No experiment tests the stated central premise of transfer to "unknown or cross-task scenarios". For example, nothing calibrates or tunes on one task and tests on another. The baselines are also not allowed this: SWEET could be calibrated per task or per domain, and that would be the natural strong baseline.
- The claim "we are the first to systematically investigate" cross-task watermarking is overstated. SWEET, EWD, AW and related works already evaluate across code, NLG and math, and mixed-modality settings are discussed in cited surveys.
- Missing baselines include unbiased or distortion-free methods (Hu et al., STA-1/STA-M, which are cited but not compared) and per-task calibrated SWEET.

### 5. The robustness evaluation is thin and misses the attack that matters most

- Only back-translation and one LLM paraphrase (a 7B model) are used, mostly on MATH-500. The post-attack AUROC of 91.9 for CATMark versus 91.7 for EWD (Table 4) is a negligible, statistically indistinguishable difference. This does not support "superior robustness".
- There are no code-specific attacks, although code is the paper's focus. Comment removal, identifier renaming, reformatting and refactoring are natural attacks.
  - Figure 4b suggests the watermark is concentrated in comment tokens, since those have higher entropy. An attacker who deletes comments would therefore remove most of the signal. This is a key weakness for the code-with-comments setting and should be tested.
- There is no length analysis (AUROC versus number of tokens), no test of false positives on human-written text or on non-watermarked LLM text, and no adaptive attacks against the clustering or thresholding.
- Detection requires a white-box forward pass through the generating LLM (~1 s per sample). This should be stated clearly as a deployment limitation, shared with SWEET and EWD.

### 6. Presentation and reproducibility

- Several metric names are missing or garbled in the PDF. For example, the Pass@1 column label is blank in Tables 1 and 6, and the headers in Table 8 and the Figure 3/4 captions are incomplete.
- Detection is described as "a single global threshold with entropy-weighted scoring", but the contributions section and Figure 2 emphasize context-aware thresholds. This makes it unclear which part of the novelty reaches the detector.
- Experimental details are scattered or missing:
  - the sampling setup;
  - the number of generations per prompt;
  - how negative (human or unwatermarked) samples are constructed for AUROC;
  - the z-score threshold;
  - the SWEET calibration procedure.
- No code release is mentioned. The appendix title uses a different expansion of the acronym ("Adaptive Entropy Threshold Watermarking").

## Overall Assessment

The problem is real and the idea of an online, data-driven per-context threshold is reasonable and cheap. However, the central claims are not adequately supported:

- The theory compares lower bounds for a quantity not used by the deployed detector.
- The "semantic state" clustering is never validated.
- The quality and detection gains over the best baselines (SWEET-1.2, EWD) are within about one point and without significance testing.
- The paper's own ablation and Llama tables contradict the "best in both" narrative.
- The ablation values for the QBT baseline (46.0 on MATH-500) look anomalous.
- The "cross-task" setting is a set of independent single-task runs. It never evaluates actual task switching, task transfer, or the most relevant code attacks.

## Questions for the Authors

1. What is the F1 or purity of the learned clusters against ground-truth segment types in HumanEval and MBPP outputs? How large does K get, and how do results change if you cluster on entropy alone, or use a fixed K?
2. Do prototypes persist across prompts, batches and users? Please clarify "Globals … per task". Is output independent of batch composition?
3. Why does QBT alone score 46.0 on MATH-500 (below KGW at 68.6)? Is the baseline SWEET with a calibrated threshold, per SWEET's own protocol, included anywhere?
4. Please add unwatermarked rows to Table 1, define the "±" values, state the decoding settings, and report statistical tests.
5. What are the empirical FPR at your z-threshold, on both human text and non-watermarked LLM text? What is the AUROC versus length?
6. How does detection hold up when comments are stripped, identifiers are renamed, or code is reformatted?
7. How does the mismatch between per-cluster generation thresholds and the global detection threshold affect the z-score? Can you give a version of Theorem 1/2 that applies to the actual detector and to Shannon entropy?
8. Why do the baseline numbers differ between Table 1 and Table 4, and why does QBT+EWD beat full CATMark on MBPP detection?

## Scores (EMNLP-style)

- **Soundness:** 2.5/5. The method is plausible, but the theory is a loose fit, the evidence is mixed and inconsistent, and key validations are missing.
- **Excitement / Novelty:** 2.5–3/5. This is an incremental combination of SWEET-style thresholding, EWD weighting, and online clustering.
- **Overall recommendation:** 2.5–3/5 (borderline, leaning reject in the current form; Findings-level at best). Substantive revisions are needed before the claims are supported.
- **Reproducibility:** 2.5/5. Algorithms are given, but decoding settings, evaluation protocol and code are missing.
- **Confidence:** 4/5.

## Ethics / Limitations

There are no significant ethical concerns. The limitations section is reasonable but should also discuss white-box detection, comment-removal and code-transformation attacks, and statefulness of the prototypes across requests.

# Review: SymboLLM-FE: LLM-Accelerated Symbolic Regression for Automated Feature Engineering on Tabular Data

## Summary

The paper proposes SymboLLM-FE, a two-stage AutoFE pipeline.

1. **Stage 1.** Features are ranked by Spearman correlation with the target. An "expanding-sliding window" over the ranked list produces O(n²) feature subsets. A gplearn genetic-programming symbolic regressor is fit on each subset, which yields a repository of (subset, performance, formula) triples.
2. **Stage 2.** The formulas and their MAE are put into a prompt. An LLM writes pandas code to create or drop features, guided by validation feedback from a downstream predictor.

The authors claim better predictive performance than traditional and LLM-based AutoFE, better interpretability, and fewer LLM calls (about 4). Evaluation covers six OpenML/Kaggle datasets with four downstream models, four Kaggle competitions, an LLM-backbone comparison, and an ablation.

## Strengths

- The idea is simple and sensible. It uses symbolic regression to give the LLM statistically grounded candidates, rather than having the LLM propose features open-endedly. The small number of LLM calls is a real practical advantage over OCTree and FEBP.
- The evaluation spans several downstream models (CatBoost, XGBoost, MLP, TabPFN) and three metrics per task type. The appendix tables are fairly complete.
- Code and prompts are released, and hyperparameters are listed.
- The paper is readable, and Table 4 gives cost numbers.

## Weaknesses

### 1. The empirical gains are small and not shown to be significant

- Section 5.2 claims "statistically significant improvements … (average gain of 1.23%)". No significance test, p-value, or confidence interval appears anywhere.
- In Table 2 (TabPFN), most differences are well within one standard deviation. Examples:
  - Credit-g: 77.00±1.63 vs. baseline 77.03±0.47, so SymboLLM-FE is actually below baseline and below CAAFE (78.00).
  - Spaceship: 81.27±1.31 vs. 80.79±1.27.
  - Cmc: 57.97±0.73 vs. 57.85±0.89.
- Results use only three seeds (C.5), which is too few for the claim.
- The "1.23% average gain" is not defined. It is unclear whether it is relative or absolute, or over which datasets and models.
- The appendix claims SymboLLM-FE "achieves the most best and second-best results" and "consistently improves or maintains top performance". Tables 10 and 11 do not support this:
  - **Table 10, MLP.** SymboLLM-FE is below baseline on Spaceship (76.43±13.90 vs. 77.46) and is not best on Tesla, where OcTree gets 11.20.
  - **Table 10, XGBoost.** It is not best on Tesla.
  - **Table 10, CatBoost.** It is not best on Credit-g or Academic.
  - **Table 11.** It loses on Credit-g, Spaceship (CatBoost), Academic, and MLP for several datasets.
- The MLP results have extreme variance (e.g., ±11.39, ±17.61, ±13.90), so they are essentially uninformative.
- On the Kaggle tasks (Fig. 3), the bars are visually almost indistinguishable. The "2.5pp average improvement" is not reproduced by any table. No numbers, seeds, or variance are given, and a Kaggle leaderboard rank would be more meaningful.

### 2. Possible validation and test leakage, and an unclear protocol

- The prompt template in Appendix B says "The MAE indicates the performance of the Symbolic Regressor model on the **test set**". Section 4 claims the training set alone is used for symbolic regression and the test set is reserved for final evaluation. If the formula MAEs shown to the LLM come from the test set, this is leakage. At minimum it is a contradiction that must be resolved.
- Section 4 says the LLM loop is guided by validation scores, and the test set is also used in "Downstream Predictor Performance Validation". The exact data flow is hard to follow.
- Baselines may not have received the same tuning budget, validation use, or number of iterations. Hyperparameter grids appear only for downstream models. How the AutoFE baselines were configured is not stated, e.g., the number of features for OpenFE, or the iteration counts for CAAFE and OcTree.
- "Fold-wise cross-validation" is mentioned, but it is not clear how the symbolic regression, LLM, and predictor are nested within folds. A loop that selects the best validation score across multiple LLM rounds on a small validation set (Credit-g has 1,000 samples) is prone to selection bias.

### 3. The central efficiency claim is overstated and partly a straw man

- The reduction from O(2ⁿ) to O(n²) is relative to exhaustive subset enumeration, which no one does. The comparison is not against realistic alternatives such as random subsets or the full feature set. The headline complexity claim therefore says little.
- The derived bound (Eq. 2) is arithmetic, but each of the ~n²/8 subsets still requires a full GP run with a population of 20,000, 120 generations, and tournament size 100 (Table 6). This is expensive:
  - 25–30 minutes for 36 and 33 features (Table 4).
  - For high-dimensional tabular data (hundreds of features) it would be infeasible. The Limitations section concedes "prohibitive time overhead", which conflicts with the "exceptional time cost" language in Sec. 5.3.
- Sec. 5.5 claims runtime "scales linearly with formulas and dataset size", but only six data points are given. Ailerons (171 formulas, 30.24 min) vs. Academic (190 formulas, 25.34 min) is not monotone.
- "Approximately four API calls" depends on the dataset: Table 4 shows 2–5 calls and Table 1 shows 4. The Table 1 comparison is not described: which dataset, which downstream model, what "Score" means, and why "Generated Features" for LLM-RANK is "–". Total wall-clock time and token cost are not compared with baselines. The FEBP comparison (43.71 min) comes from another paper and appears to be on different hardware and datasets.
- Fewer LLM calls is not the same as lower cost. Total cost, including the CPU time for GP, should be compared on the same datasets and hardware.

### 4. Inconsistencies in the method description

- Sec. 4.1 sorts features in monotonic *ascending* order of correlation, so the first window of size ⌊n/2⌋ contains the *least* target-correlated features. Figure 2 and the Limitations say "descending order of importance". Which is correct?
- It is unclear whether Spearman correlation is computed on signed or absolute values. Strong negative correlations would be ranked last in a signed ascending ordering.
- The sliding-window scheme assumes that useful interactions involve features adjacent in marginal-correlation rank. This is a strong and unjustified assumption, and the paper acknowledges it in the Limitations. Features that matter only through interactions have low marginal Spearman correlation and are systematically misplaced. No experiment tests this, e.g., on synthetic data with known XOR or product interactions.
- Appendix A.4 refers to "Eq. (1)" for the parsimony penalty, but this is Eq. (4). Eq. (4) also adds Ω·size to MSE, which is scale-dependent, so a single grid {0.005…0.05} is odd across datasets with different target scales.
- Gplearn's protected operators (e.g., div returning 1, inv returning 0, sin/cos/tan on raw features) produce formulas whose "interpretability" is questionable.
- The paper says it uses "SymbolicClassifier" for classification. This fits a logistic-transformed GP output, so the "MAE" of formulas in the prompt for classification tasks is not well defined. It is also unclear how multi-class tasks (Cmc, Academic) are handled.

### 5. The main motivational claims are not tested

- **Interpretability.** This is the paper's central selling point, yet there is no quantitative or human evaluation. Only one hand-picked example is shown (Infection_Exposure_Risk in Fig. 1, which looks like a schematic rather than an actual output).
  - There are no sample outputs on the real datasets, no formula-complexity statistics, and no user study.
  - It is not shown that the LLM's rewrite is faithful to the formula or that the final features are more interpretable than CAAFE's.
  - Symbolic regression expressions are not inherently interpretable.
  - Feature *names* alone (a feature of LLM-based AutoFE too) do not establish interpretability. A feature generated by the LLM after seeing formulas may not correspond to the formula.
- **Hallucination and bias.** The paper claims it "eliminates the generation of spurious or hallucinated features" (Sec. 5.3) and "eliminates hallucination" (Sec. 4.2). This is asserted, not measured. The LLM still writes arbitrary Python code and can ignore the formulas. The prompt explicitly asks it to go beyond the formulas ("you should not simply convert all formulas", "make full use of your prior knowledge"), which is exactly where hallucination could occur. Nothing measures execution failure rates, invalid features, or bias or fairness.
- **Introduction.** The introduction's "empirical analysis" identifying LLM-AutoFE weaknesses (contribution 1) amounts to Table 1, whose setup is undescribed. It is not a real analysis. The statement that LLM-based AutoFE "causes a drop in model performance" is based on one cell (LLM-RANK, which is a feature selector, not a generator).
- The "statistical prior-grounded LLM refinement mechanism" and "rigorous feature control and de-redundancy mechanisms" (Sec. 4.2) are described in vague terms ("prompt-independent constraints", "LLM serves as a semantic filter"). No algorithm box, no feature-count statistics, and no analysis of how many features are dropped are given. Table 1 reports 70 features for SymboLLM-FE vs. 30 for CAAFE and LLM-FE, so "compact" is relative.

### 6. Weak or confounded ablation and generalization analyses

- Fig. 4 reports a single bar per variant on an unspecified dataset and model, with no error bars. The text says "independent random seeds" and Appendix F says the full method has "the lowest standard deviation", but the figure shows no variance. Differences are 0.1–1.3 points, comparable to the noise seen in Table 2. Removing Spearman gives 76.07 vs. the baseline's 75.81, which is a negligible difference.
- Missing ablations:
  - A random-subset or full-feature symbolic regression variant.
  - An LLM-only variant that sees feature names and data but no formulas. This is the key control for the claim that symbolic regression, rather than the LLM alone, helps.
  - A variant that adds the raw symbolic formulas directly as features, without the LLM.
  - Sensitivity to GP hyperparameters, the number of formulas fed to the prompt, and the number of LLM rounds.
- The model comparison (Table 3) confounds LLM capability with other factors. It does not say which dataset is used, whether the numbers are comparable with Table 2, or how many runs there are. The claim that effectiveness "is closely related to the LLM's reasoning capability" is a conjecture. A stronger LLM could simply write better pandas code, and no analysis is given. Only three backbones are used, GPT-4 vs. o1 vs. DeepSeek-R1, none of them open small models. Stronger LLMs also help the LLM-only baselines, which are not run with the same backbones. Which LLM is used for the baselines in Table 2?
- Table 3 numbers (CatBoost 75–78%, TabPFN 76.8–79.5%) do not match any single column of Table 2 or Table 10. It is unclear whether they are averages. "Significantly outperform" (Sec. 5.4) is again not tested.

### 7. Limited and potentially unrepresentative benchmarks

- Six small datasets (1,000–12,250 rows, 8–36 features) are used. Credit-g, Cmc, and Spaceship are saturated benchmarks with high variance. Several standard AutoFE benchmarks used in CAAFE, OpenFE, and OCTree (e.g., larger OpenML suites) are missing, as is any dataset with 100+ features.
- Tesla stock data with Open/High/Low/Close features is close to a leakage or trivial-relationship problem, since a close price is nearly determined by the others. The "factor mining" and financial-regulatory motivation in the introduction is never tested.
- The "Spaceship" and "Academic" datasets are Kaggle datasets, but the paper does not say how splits were created or how Kaggle private/public leaderboard scores (Fig. 3) were obtained.
- Metrics in the main table (accuracy, RMSE) and the appendix (ROC-AUC, MAE) tell different stories, e.g., SymboLLM-FE looks much stronger on ROC-AUC with CatBoost and TabPFN than on accuracy. The paper does not discuss the differences. F1 and R² are said to be reported but never shown.
- Using TabPFN as the headline downstream model is unusual for AutoFE evaluation. TabPFN is meant to handle raw features without engineering and has dataset-size limits.
